questions.q: What does account containment involve, beyond just changing the password?
options: Disabling the account and revoking active sessions/tokens, since a stolen session can outlive a password reset
Reinstalling the operating system on the user's machine
Only ever deleting the account permanently
Blocking the account's IP address at the firewall only
questions.explain: A password reset alone doesn't invalidate an already-authenticated session or stolen token — those have to be revoked separately.

options: Isolating the compromised machine from the network while leaving it running for investigation
Immediately deleting all accounts that ever logged into that machine
Resetting every password in the organization
Shipping the machine to a third-party vendor for repair
questions.explain: Host containment isolates the machine's network access, as covered in the EDR isolation lesson, while keeping it live for investigation.

questions.q: If an attacker is using a compromised account from a compromised host, why does disabling only the account leave the incident half-contained?
options: The attacker still has a foothold on the infected machine, which can harvest different credentials or move laterally
Disabling an account always re-enables itself automatically after a few minutes
Disabling an account also automatically isolates every host on the network
Host containment is never necessary in any scenario
questions.explain: Malware or a backdoor on the host can harvest a different account or spread further even after the first account is disabled.

questions.q: If an attacker is using a compromised account from a compromised host, why does isolating only the host leave the incident half-contained?
options: There is no risk left once the host is isolated
Isolating a host always disables every account that ever used it
Host isolation makes stolen credentials stop working automatically
The attacker can still use the stolen credentials to log in from a different device or location entirely, especially for a cloud/SaaS account
questions.explain: A cloud account isn't tied to one infected device, so stolen credentials can still be used from anywhere until the account itself is contained.

questions.q: In the phishing example, what two actions does the SOC need to take at the same time?
options: Only isolate the laptop, since the account will become safe automatically
Delete the user's account and laptop permanently with no further investigation
Only disable the Office 365 account, since the laptop isn't actually relevant
Disable the Office 365 account and revoke its sessions, AND isolate the infected laptop via EDR
questions.explain: Both the stolen identity and the infected machine need to be contained together, since each one alone leaves a path open.
